scenario: The warehouse release pipeline was built in the classic web editor. Nobody can review changes to it, and its history is unclear.
stem: What is the main benefit of rebuilding it as a YAML pipeline?
options: YAML pipelines run faster
The pipeline lives in the repository, so it is versioned, reviewed in pull requests and rebuilt from source like the code it ships
YAML pipelines need no agents
Classic pipelines cannot deploy to Azure
explanation: Pipeline-as-code brings the same controls as application code: history, review and reproducibility. Speed and agent use are the same, and classic pipelines can deploy to Azure - they are just opaque.

scenario: A fix passed in test but failed in production. The pipeline rebuilt the code separately for each environment and picked up a newer dependency the second time.
stem: What should the pipeline do instead?
options: Rebuild more carefully with pinned versions each time
Build once, publish the artefact, and deploy that same artefact to test and then production
Skip the test environment
Build only in production
explanation: Promoting one artefact guarantees production runs exactly what was tested. Pinning helps, but separate builds can still differ. Skipping test or building only in production removes the check entirely.

scenario: The pipeline must deploy to a server in the warehouse office that has no inbound internet access.
options: A Microsoft-hosted agent, which can reach any network
A self-hosted agent in the office, which makes outbound connections to Azure DevOps and deploys locally
Open RDP on the server so the hosted agent can connect in
No agent is needed for on-premises deployments
explanation: Hosted agents run on the internet and cannot reach private networks. A self-hosted agent inside the network pulls jobs over outbound HTTPS, so no inbound ports are opened. Opening RDP to the internet undoes Module 4.

scenario: A developer worries that anyone could remove the production approval by editing azure-pipelines.yml in a pull request.
stem: Where should the production approval be configured?
options: As a step in the YAML file
On the warehouse-prod environment's approvals and checks, which the YAML cannot override
In the README
On the build stage
explanation: Checks on an environment are enforced by Azure DevOps whenever a deployment job targets it, regardless of what the pipeline file says. A step in the YAML can be deleted in the same pull request that ships the risky change.

scenario: Deployments stopped because the service principal secret behind the Azure service connection expired.
options: Create a new secret with the longest possible expiry
Recreate the service connection with workload identity federation, scoped to one resource group
Use a personal account for the connection
Store the secret in a variable group
explanation: Federation lets the pipeline exchange its own token for an Azure token, so there is no secret to expire or leak. Scoping it narrowly limits what a compromised pipeline could do. Longer expiries, personal accounts and variable groups keep the underlying problem.

scenario: One service connection with Owner on the whole subscription is shared by every pipeline in the project.
stem: What is the risk, and the fix?
options: No risk, since only pipelines use it

Any pipeline - or anyone who can edit one - can change anything in the subscription; use one federated connection per environment scoped to its resource group, restrict which pipelines can use it, and add checks on production
It is slower than several connections
It prevents approvals
explanation: A pipeline can do whatever its connection allows, so a broad, shared connection turns any pipeline edit into subscription-wide power. Narrow scope, pipeline permissions and checks on production connections apply least privilege to CI/CD.

scenario: Security wants dependency scanning in all 30 pipelines, and wants to be sure teams cannot drop it.
options: Email every team asking them to add a scanning step
An extends template in a shared repository that includes the mandatory scan, which every pipeline must extend
Copy the step into each pipeline once
Run scans manually each month
explanation: An extends template defines the pipeline's structure, including mandatory steps teams cannot remove, and changes roll out from one place. Emails and one-off copies drift, and monthly manual scans miss everything between them.

scenario: The self-hosted build agent has run for three years under an admin account, with old tools and files from previous builds.
options: Leave it; it works
Move to Managed DevOps Pools or ephemeral agents where possible, and otherwise patch, clean and run the agent with least privilege
Share its admin password with the team
Install more tools on it
explanation: Long-lived agents accumulate state, stale tools and excessive privilege, and a compromise gives an attacker a trusted path into deployments. Managed or ephemeral agents start clean each time; any remaining self-hosted agent needs patching and least privilege.
